title: Make the site search-ready before decorating it
metaTitle: SEO for a new website, before polish
excerpt: A new site is search-ready when titles, headings, speed, and a plain sentence say what the company is. Decoration on a vague page does not earn the click.
alt: A dim desk with an iMac showing a code editor beside a portfolio page, a second monitor with a mountain wallpaper, and a lit lamp. The page on screen is what search has to understand.
caption: The page has to say what the company is before the room around it gets busier. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What makes a new website search-ready?
faqs.answer: A sentence that says what the company is, a unique title and one clear heading on each page, a primary action that goes somewhere real, and a page that can meet Core Web Vitals before heavy decoration is added. Search engines and first-time visitors are both asking what this is. A vague page with a handsome surface still has no answer.

faqs.question: What should the title element do?
faqs.answer: Describe that specific page, in concise language, and match the visible heading. Google's title-link guidance warns against vague labels such as Home and against repeating the same phrase to chase a query. When the title, the heading, and the page disagree, Google may show a different title link.

faqs.question: When should visual decoration be added?
faqs.answer: After the sentence, the titles, the primary action, and a speed check. Illustration, motion, and custom type are welcome when they support that sentence. They do not repair a hero that could belong to any company in the category. If the offer is slow to appear on a phone, remove something before you add more.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
SEO for a new website starts with titles, headings, speed, and a sentence that says what the company is. Decoration on top of a vague page does not rank, and it does not convert. Search engines and first-time visitors are both trying to answer the same question: what is this, and why should I stay.

The polish can wait until that answer is on the page. A type treatment, a motion study, and a custom illustration will not repair a title that says "Home" or a hero that could belong to any company in the category.

## Say what the company is

The first sentence a stranger meets should name the buyer and the thing you make. "Hanabi designs and builds websites and product interfaces for founders" is that kind of sentence. A poetic brand line can sit beside it. The poetic line cannot be the only line.

Write the sentence before you open a layout file. If you cannot say it in one breath, the page will pad it with abstractions. People do not search for a digital impression. They search for a partner, a product, or a fix. The sentence should be willing to use those words.

Put the same clarity in the opening of the page, not only in a meta description nobody sees until after the click. A visitor with no prior context should leave the first screen able to say what you make and who it is for. A page written so a crawler might guess the topic, while a person still cannot, wastes the visit.

## Titles and headings before ornaments

Every page needs its own title element, and the title should describe that page. [Google's documentation on title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) says the title is often the main clue people use to choose a result, and it warns against vague labels such as "Home." It also warns against stuffing the title with repeats of the same phrase. A concise, specific title is the whole craft.

Write the title as a promise the page keeps. If the page is about a store migration, the title should say so. If the page is the company home, the title can carry the search language while the visible heading stays more particular. Google generates the title link from several sources, including the title element, the visible heading, and other prominent text. When those disagree, or when the title is boilerplate reused across the site, Google may show something else. Alignment is the practical fix. One clear heading, more prominent than the labels around it, describing the page you actually published.

Headings below that are the real sections: the offer, the work, the way an engagement runs, the questions buyers ask. Decorative words in small type can exist. They should not be the only structure. A screen reader and a hurried founder both depend on the headings to tell the truth.

## Speed is part of being findable

A search-ready page is a fast page. [Google's Core Web Vitals](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/core-web-vitals) are the thresholds to design toward. Largest Contentful Paint within 2.5 seconds, Interaction to Next Paint within 200 milliseconds, and Cumulative Layout Shift under 0.1. Those figures are the published "good" bar, and they are easier to hit before the decorative layer arrives.

Heavy video in the first screen, a font that delays the headline, and images without a stable size are the usual ways a young site misses the bar. Add them only when they explain something the sentence could not. A still photograph with known dimensions is often the faster, calmer choice. Motion, if you use it, should show a relationship or a state, and it should have a reduced version for people who ask for less movement.

Treat speed as a launch check, not as a post-launch apology. Look at the page on a phone, on an ordinary connection, and see whether the offer appears before you start to wonder if the site is broken. If it does not, remove something. Adding a preloader does not count as a fix.

## One page, one job

A new site is easier to understand when each URL has one intent. The home page says who it is for and how to start. A project page says what the project was. An article answers one question a buyer actually has. A page that tries to rank for every service, in every industry, becomes a brochure with no center.

Internal links should point at the next useful page, from a sentence that earns the click. A footer that lists every URL on the site is a map. It is a weak substitute for one honest link in the paragraph where the reader needs it. Until a service has its own page, link to the real section that describes the work.

Name the proof you can actually show. Public projects, a clear description of the stack, a portal where files live after delivery. Leave invented metrics off the page. A specific project a person can look at is stronger than a rounded claim about growth.

## The order of work

Do the search-ready layer in this order, and refuse to skip ahead because a visual idea is more fun.

1. Write the sentence that says what the company is, and put it where the first screen can carry it.
2. Write a unique title and one clear heading for each page you intend to publish.
3. Mark the primary action and the place it goes: a call, a form, or an email someone answers.
4. Check the page against the vitals thresholds before you add the heavy decorative idea.
5. Add the visual layer that supports the sentence. Cut the layer that competes with it.
6. Read the page on a phone, with the titles visible in a search-result preview, and see if you would click your own link.

Decoration is welcome after step five. It is the part people remember. It works when the page already tells the truth quickly. A beautiful vague page is still vague, and neither a crawler nor a buyer has a reason to prefer it.

Hanabi's design and build work treats this order as part of the craft, not as a separate marketing phase. If you want that sequence applied to a company site, start with [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services).

Titles deserve their own pass once the page has something to promise. [Titles and descriptions that earn the click](/blog/titles-that-earn-the-click) is the next piece, because a true sentence still has to survive as a title link someone chooses.
